plan.topic: Tirzepatide constipation: how common it was in the trials vs placebo, why it happens (slower gut movement and eating and drinking less), and a food-first plan (fluids, fibre built up gradually, movement, routine), plus when to call your prescriber
plan.angle:
Lane A (log 'lane: A'). Put it in the 'Life on Tirzepatide' playlist, 8–12 min, 14:00 ET.

Opening: the first spoken sentence answers the title with a 'you' scenario, e.g. 'Feeling backed up on tirzepatide? You're not alone. Constipation was one of the most common side effects in the trials, and a few simple, steady habits are what experts recommend.'

Chapters, named after searched questions:
(1) How common is constipation on tirzepatide? Use SURMOUNT-1 per-arm rates vs placebo, with group sizes and 72 weeks. Population: adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes. Fact-checker: confirm the 11.7% / 16.8% / 17.1% vs 5.8% figures against NEJM 2022 and the current Zepbound label, which was revised 28 Aug 2026. Add one SURPASS line, labelled 'type 2 diabetes'.
(2) Why does it happen? Use the label's wording that tirzepatide can delay gastric emptying. Smaller meals and lower fluid intake are a leading explanation, not a certainty.
(3) Does fibre help or hurt? Build fibre up gradually and pair it with fluids. Quote the advisory's 'avoiding fatty or high fiber foods during the first few days of treatment' only at that exact scope (easing nausea), and explain why it doesn't conflict.
(4) How much should I drink? Sip through the day, unless you've been told to limit fluids.
(5) Does movement help? A walk and a regular routine are our own tips, with no source tag.
(6) What about laxatives or supplements? Ask your pharmacist or prescriber before using any. No product names or doses.
(7) When to call your prescriber? Use the label's warning signs in its exact wording: severe stomach pain that won't go away, and vomiting or diarrhoea with signs of dehydration. Add 'contact your healthcare provider'.

All habits are 'recommended', never 'proven on tirzepatide'.

Re-hook every 45–75 s. One subscribe ask, after the 'what helps' payoff. Include 'Not personal advice', 'don't stop, switch or change your medicines on your own' and the full prescriber line. No dosing or titration talk, and no spoken titles.

Ending: 'There's a video I'd watch next, linked in the description.' The publisher links 'What to Eat on Tirzepatide'.

Thumbnail: before-after layout, 4 words or fewer (e.g. 'Gut Back on Track'), one labelled, relieved tummy character.
plan.why: Next Lane A topic in the queue ('fibre and constipation'). It's a very common side effect with high search demand, it rests on the label, the trial data and the advisory, and it strengthens the Life on Tirzepatide suggested-video cluster.

package.description:
Quick answer: In SURMOUNT-1 (adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes), constipation was reported by 11.7–17.1% across tirzepatide dose groups vs 5.8% on placebo over 72 weeks. Gut side effects were mostly mild to moderate, mainly during dose increases. Leading explanation: slower stomach emptying plus eating and drinking less.

Not personal advice. Ask your pharmacist or prescriber before any laxative or supplement. Don't stop, switch or change your medicines on your own. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether tirzepatide is right for you.

Sources:
1. Jastreboff AM et al. NEJM 2022 (SURMOUNT-1): https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35658024/
2. Zepbound Prescribing Information, Eli Lilly: https://pi.lilly.com/us/zepbound-uspi.pdf
3. Mozaffarian D et al. Am J Clin Nutr 2025: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40450457/
4. NIDDK, Treatment for Constipation: https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/constipation/treatment

scenes.section: How common is constipation on tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: So, how common is it really? Let's go to the biggest tirzepatide weight trial in people without diabetes, called SURMOUNT One.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter card with a searched question

scenes.section: How common is constipation on tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: It enrolled two thousand five hundred and thirty-nine adults with obesity, or with overweight plus a weight-related condition. None of them had diabetes, and they were followed for seventy-two weeks.

scenes.section: How common is constipation on tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: Each person was randomly assigned to one of three tirzepatide doses or a placebo, with about six hundred and thirty to six hundred and forty-three people per group.

scenes.section: How common is constipation on tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: Those are trial groups, not dosing advice.

scenes.section: How common is constipation on tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: Here's who reported constipation over those seventy-two weeks. On placebo: five point eight percent.

visual.stock_query: big number on calm blue card

scenes.section: How common is constipation on tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: On the five milligram dose of tirzepatide: sixteen point eight percent.

scenes.section: How common is constipation on tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: On ten milligrams: seventeen point one percent.

scenes.section: How common is constipation on tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: And on fifteen milligrams: eleven point seven percent.
scenes.retention_device: Stat reveal sets up the twist

scenes.section: How common is constipation on tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: In human terms, that's roughly one person in six in the two lower-dose groups, versus about one in seventeen on placebo.

visual.stock_query: six friends at dinner table smiling

scenes.section: How common is constipation on tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: But did you spot the twist? The highest dose had the lowest rate of the three tirzepatide groups. So it wasn't simply 'more medicine, more constipation'.

visual.stock_query: surprised character looking at bar chart

scenes.retention_device: Re-hook: surprising pattern in the data

scenes.section: How common is constipation on tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: The trial wasn't designed to explain that, so we won't guess. The useful takeaway: it was common in every tirzepatide group.

scenes.section: How common is constipation on tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: Here's the reassuring part. The researchers reported that most gut side effects were mild to moderate, and they happened mainly during the trial's dose-increase phase, in the early months.

visual.stock_query: calendar with early weeks highlighted gently

scenes.section: How common is constipation on tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: What if you have type 2 diabetes? In the type 2 diabetes trials pooled in the Mounjaro label, constipation was reported by about six to seven percent on tirzepatide, compared with about one percent on placebo.

visual.stat_label: Type 2 diabetes trials: tirzepatide vs placebo

scenes.section: How common is constipation on tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: Those are separate trials, with different people and lengths, so don't compare them head to head with SURMOUNT One.

visual.stock_query: two separate study books side by side

scenes.section: How common is constipation on tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: So it's common, and usually mild. But why would a medicine that quiets your appetite change your bathroom schedule at all?
The answer starts with two hormones your gut already makes when you eat, G L P one and G I P. Tirzepatide acts on the receptors for both.
scenes.on_screen_text: Two gut hormones: GLP-1 and GIP

visual.stock_query: two friendly hormone characters in gut

scenes.retention_device: Chapter card with a searched question

scenes.narration: One effect is written right into the prescribing information. Tirzepatide delays gastric emptying. In plain words, food leaves your stomach more slowly.

visual.stock_query: stomach character with slow traffic light

scenes.narration: That's part of why you feel full sooner and stay full longer. Great for appetite. But it also means the first stage of digestion runs at a slower pace.
And here's a hopeful detail from the label: the delay is largest after the first dose, and it diminishes over time.
The second piece is simpler. You're eating less. Sometimes a lot less.
Picture Sam's day now. Half a yoghurt for breakfast. A few crackers at lunch. And a water bottle that comes home still full, because Sam just isn't thirsty.

visual.stock_query: full water bottle forgotten on desk

scenes.narration: Less food usually means less fibre and less bulk. And not eating enough fibre and not drinking enough liquids are both well-known causes of constipation in general.

visual.stock_query: empty fibre bowl and empty glass

scenes.narration: Put together, slower stomach emptying plus smaller meals and fewer fluids is the leading explanation. It isn't fully proven for tirzepatide. But it points straight at what you can change.
So the obvious fix is to load up on fibre, right? This is where it gets tricky.

visual.stock_query: character about to eat giant bran bowl

scenes.retention_device: 'But here's where it gets tricky' re-hook into the main loop

scenes.narration: Does fibre help or hurt? Mostly, it helps. Fibre adds bulk and helps keep stool soft, so it's easier to pass.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter card with a searched question

scenes.narration: But imagine Sam going from almost no fibre to a giant bowl of bran cereal overnight. A sudden jump like that can bring gas and bloating. Exactly what Sam didn't need.

visual.stock_query: puffy bloated cartoon tummy, mildly annoyed

scenes.retention_device: Payoff part one of the fibre loop

scenes.narration: Think of fibre as a sponge. A sponge only works when there's water to soak up. Fibre works better when you drink enough fluids alongside it.
That's the backfire. The fix isn't more fibre, fast. It's more fibre, slowly, with fluids.

visual.myth: Just eat lots more fibre, fast
visual.fact: Build fibre up gradually, with fluids

scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the 'backfire' half of the loop

scenes.narration: Now, that official line I mentioned. A joint advisory on GLP-1 treatment from four lifestyle medicine, nutrition and obesity organisations suggests, quote, 'avoiding fatty or high fiber foods during the first few days of treatment'.

visual.quote: avoiding fatty or high fiber foods during the first few days of treatment
visual.attribution: Joint GLP-1 nutrition advisory (ACLM, ASN, OMA, TOS), 2025

scenes.retention_device: Pays off the 'seems to say the opposite' tease

scenes.narration: Read the scope carefully. That's about the first few days, and it's about easing nausea while your stomach adjusts. It isn't a rule to avoid fibre for good.

visual.stock_query: magnifying glass on calendar first days

scenes.narration: So there's no conflict. Early on, gentler foods to help with nausea. Then, build fibre back up step by step, with fluids, to keep things moving.

visual.stock_query: two arrows joining into one path

scenes.narration: What does step by step look like? The NIH advice is to add fibre a little at a time. One easy way: add one fibre-rich food, and give your gut a few days before adding the next.

visual.stock_query: stairs made of fruit and oats

scenes.narration: Some easy places to start: oats or berries at breakfast, beans or lentils in a soup, vegetables next to your protein, or a piece of fruit like a pear or a kiwi as a snack.

visual.stock_query: colourful bowl of oats and berries

scenes.narration: Your plate is smaller now, so make a few of those bites high in fibre, alongside your protein.

visual.stock_query: small plate with salmon and veg

scenes.narration: And that sponge needs water. So, how much should you actually drink?
Honest answer: there's no single number that fits everyone. It depends on your body, the weather, how active you are and your health.
A simple habit is to sip through the day, rather than trying to gulp a lot at once. Big gulps may feel uncomfortable when your stomach is emptying slowly.

visual.stock_query: person sipping water at desk calmly

scenes.narration: Water counts. So do other liquids, like clear soups, which can help fibre do its job.

visual.stock_query: warm bowl of clear vegetable soup

scenes.narration: One important exception. If a doctor has told you to limit fluids, for example because of a heart or kidney condition, follow that advice instead.

visual.stock_query: doctor and patient reviewing a plan

scenes.narration: There's a second reason fluids matter on tirzepatide. The prescribing information warns that vomiting or diarrhoea can lead to a loss of fluids, and kidney problems have been reported in people who became dehydrated.
Sam tries something small: the water bottle stays on the desk, and gets refilled at lunch. No strict rules. Just a visible cue.

visual.stock_query: water bottle on desk being refilled

scenes.narration: Fibre and fluids are two legs of a three-legged stool. Yes, pun intended. The third leg costs nothing, and you can start it today.

visual.stock_query: three-legged stool with one leg missing

scenes.narration: Movement. A gentle walk after a meal is a simple habit worth trying; general constipation guidance includes being physically active.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter card, payoff of the cliffhanger

scenes.narration: It doesn't need to be a workout. Ten minutes around the block counts.
The fourth habit is routine. Regular mealtimes, and unhurried time in the bathroom at roughly the same time each day, can help your body find a rhythm.
And when you feel the urge, don't put it off. Waiting for a better moment can make things harder later.
Picture Sam a few weeks later. Oats and berries most mornings. A bottle that actually gets emptied. A short walk after dinner. Not perfect. Just steady.
But what if you're doing all of this, and things still aren't moving? That's when people reach into the medicine cabinet. Pause first.
Before you use any laxative, stool softener or fibre supplement, ask your pharmacist or prescriber.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter card with a searched question

scenes.narration: There are several types, and they work in different ways. The right choice depends on your symptoms, your health and your other medicines.
That last part matters here. The label notes that tirzepatide's slower stomach emptying may affect how some medicines taken by mouth are absorbed.
scenes.retention_device: Surprising fact most viewers don't know

scenes.narration: So mention your tirzepatide when you ask, and list everything else you take. A two-minute chat at the pharmacy counter can save you a miserable week.
Now for the part I promised at the start: the signs that mean don't wait it out.
scenes.retention_device: Pays off the early promise of warning signs

scenes.section: When should I call my prescriber?
scenes.narration: Some symptoms mean it's time to stop managing this at home and get help.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter card with a searched question

scenes.section: When should I call my prescriber?
scenes.narration: The Zepbound medication guide is clear here. If you have severe pain in your stomach area that will not go away, with or without vomiting, it says to stop using Zepbound and call your healthcare provider right away.
scenes.on_screen_text: Severe stomach pain that won't go away: call right away

visual.stock_query: phone call to clinic, calm tone

scenes.section: When should I call my prescriber?
scenes.narration: It also says to tell your healthcare provider if you have stomach problems that are severe or will not go away.

scenes.section: When should I call my prescriber?
scenes.narration: The medication guide also says diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting can cause a loss of fluids, so it's important to drink fluids. Our own tip: if vomiting or diarrhoea comes with signs of dehydration, contact your healthcare provider. The NHS lists signs like feeling dizzy or lightheaded, peeing less often than usual, and dark yellow, strong-smelling pee.

scenes.section: When should I call my prescriber?
scenes.narration: General constipation guidance adds a few more red flags: blood in your stool, constant belly pain, not being able to pass gas, or vomiting. Those mean see a health professional right away.

visual.stock_query: calm red flag icons on card

scenes.section: When should I call my prescriber?
scenes.narration: If something feels wrong, you're never overreacting by calling. Checking in is exactly what your prescriber is there for.

scenes.section: When should I call my prescriber?
scenes.narration: Outside of what your medication guide tells you to do for those warning signs, don't stop, switch or change your medicines on your own. Make those decisions together with your prescriber.

scenes.section: When should I call my prescriber?
scenes.narration: Okay. Let's turn all of this into something you can actually use tomorrow morning.

visual.stock_query: sunrise over kitchen with water glass

scenes.narration: Here's your gut-friendly checklist. One: sip fluids through the day, unless you've been told to limit them.
Two: add fibre slowly, one food at a time, always with fluids.

visual.stock_query: oats and water glass side by side

scenes.narration: Three: move a little after meals. Four: keep a regular bathroom routine, and don't ignore the urge.
Five: ask your pharmacist or prescriber before any laxative or supplement. And six: know the warning signs, and call when you see them.
And remember the fibre paradox. Gentler foods for nausea in the first few days. Then fibre, built up step by step, with fluids. No conflict at all.

visual.fact: First few days: ease nausea. Then build fibre slowly
visual.stock_query: two paths merging into one road

scenes.retention_device: Final payoff of the main open loop

scenes.narration: To be clear, these are recommended habits for constipation in general, not something proven in a tirzepatide trial. But they're low-risk, low-cost, and they work with your body.
Imagine Sam two months in. Not every day is perfect. But that heavy, stuck feeling isn't running the show anymore, and Sam knows exactly when to pick up the phone.

visual.stock_query: Medi cheering a small win with Sam

scenes.narration: If you've felt embarrassed to bring this up, don't be. Constipation was one of the most common side effects in the trials, so it's a completely normal thing to raise.
If this helped, subscribe. We keep breaking down the practical questions about life on tirzepatide, straight from the evidence, so you walk into your next appointment ready.
scenes.retention_device: Single subscribe ask tied to a specific benefit, after the payoff

scenes.narration: Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether tirzepatide is right for you.
There's a video I'd watch next, linked in the description.
scenes.retention_device: Next-video hand-off for session watch time

factcheck.summary:
The script is accurate, safe and well hedged, so it passes. I found three minor wording issues and give exact fixes for each below.

What I checked against the sources:
- **SURMOUNT-1 (PubMed):** 2,539 adults without diabetes, four groups, 72 weeks. Constipation was 5.8% on placebo and 16.8%, 17.1% and 11.7% on the 5, 10 and 15 mg doses, which matches. The "1 in 6 vs 1 in 17" conversion is correct. The trial says GI side effects were "mostly mild to moderate, occurring primarily during dose escalation", which s18 reflects.
- **Mounjaro label (current FDA version):** pooled type 2 diabetes trials show constipation in 1% on placebo and 6%, 6% and 7% on tirzepatide, so "about six to seven percent vs about one percent" is right.
- **Joint advisory (S4):** confirmed as Mozaffarian et al., Am J Clin Nutr 2025;122(1):344-367. The quote and its "first few days, to ease nausea" scope match the channel's verified craft notes.
- **NHS dehydration page:** last reviewed 01 May 2026, and the listed signs match.
- **Other sources:** the Zepbound label statements (delayed gastric emptying that is largest after the first dose and eases over time, effects on oral medicines, and acute kidney injury with dehydration), the Medication Guide wording and the NIDDK lifestyle and red-flag advice all match their sources.

Safety: the fluid-restriction caveat (s45), the ask-before-laxatives line, the urgent-care signs, the don't-stop line (s66 handles the Medication Guide's "stop" instruction well), "Not personal advice" and the prescriber line are all present. No dosing or titration advice, Sam is clearly hypothetical, and the title is paid off.

issues.problem: The current FDA Mounjaro label is a 2026 revision (215866s041), so the year is out of date.
issues.fix: Set S3 year to "2026" and add "(current revision, 2026)" to the title, or cite https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2026/215866s041lbl.pdf alongside the Lilly PI URL.

issues.problem: The label reports kidney problems in people who became dehydrated (mostly after vomiting or diarrhoea). The card turns that into a protective-effect claim, which is stronger than the narration.
issues.fix: Change on_screen_text to: "Dehydration can strain kidneys"

issues.claim: Constipation was one of the most common side effects in the trials
issues.problem: This is accurate, but the first sentence doesn't name the trial population. It's fine as a hook, and the details come in s07–s20.
issues.fix: Optional: "Constipation was one of the most common side effects in the tirzepatide trials, and the first-line fixes recommended for constipation are simple, steady habits."
